pairs.rationale: Both introduce John in the wilderness at the beginning of his baptismal ministry. Luke additionally names his father, the priestly setting, and God's word coming to him; Mark summarizes his appearing and proclamation.

Both describe John's baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins in the Jordan setting. Luke describes movement through its region; Mark describes people coming to him and confessing sins in the river.
Luke quotes the wilderness voice commanding preparation of the Lord's way and straight paths. Saints Isaiah says paths of our God where Luke says His paths.

Both announce filled valleys, lowered mountains and hills, straightened crooked places, and smoothed rough terrain. Ravine, roads, country, and plains remain the supplied English expressions rather than a harmonized quotation.
All flesh seeing God's salvation repeats the corresponding Isaiah clause. Isaiah also mentions the Lord's glory and His spoken word, which Luke's supplied excerpt does not repeat.

Both give John's brood-of-vipers address and question about fleeing coming wrath. Luke addresses crowds coming for baptism; Matthew specifically names Pharisees and Sadducees. The audiences are not silently equated.

Both require repentance-worthy fruit and reject reliance on Abrahamic ancestry, saying God can raise Abraham's children from stones. Luke uses fruits and Matthew fruit; the shared argument remains clear.
Both place the axe at the trees' root and warn that a tree without good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire.

Both have listeners ask what they should do in response to preaching. Acts names Peter and the apostles and answers with repentance and baptism; Luke's John scene develops practical ethical answers. These are different audiences and occasions.

Both require practical provision of food and clothing to people in need. Luke specifies sharing a second tunic and food; Isaiah names hungry and naked people and additionally includes housing the homeless.

Luke's later reflection explicitly includes tax collectors baptized by John, corresponding to their coming for baptism here. The later verse does not repeat their question, so this is a same-book ministry link rather than independent testimony to the dialogue.

John forbids collection beyond authorized amounts; Zacchaeus, identified as a chief tax collector in that later scene, promises fourfold restitution for anything extorted. Both address unjust taking in tax-collection settings, without equating their speakers or occasions.

Both require contentment rather than acquisitive conduct. Luke applies it to soldiers' pay alongside bans on extortion and false accusation; Hebrews calls for a disposition free from love of money and contentment, without repeating those military-specific instructions.

Both raise the question of John's identity relative to the Christ. Luke describes the people's inward speculation; John narrates emissaries questioning him and his explicit denial. The questioners and modes of inquiry differ.
Both announce a stronger coming One, John's unworthiness to untie His sandal strap, and water baptism contrasted with Holy Spirit baptism. Luke adds fire; Mark's supplied wording does not.
Both picture the coming One clearing a threshing floor, storing wheat, and burning chaff with unquenchable fire. Winnowing fork and shovel remain the edition's distinct English terms.

Both summarize John's proclamation to the people. Luke calls it good news with many exhortations; Acts specifically describes repentance-baptism proclamation to Israel before Jesus' coming, not an exact repetition of every exhortation.

Both connect John's rebuke of Herod with Herodias, his brother's wife. Mark names Philip and quotes the marriage objection; Luke additionally refers to all Herod's evil acts without listing them here.
Both attribute John's imprisonment to Herod. Mark narrates seizure and binding in the Herodias context; Luke frames the imprisonment as an additional evil after the rebuke.

Both place an opening of heaven after Jesus' baptism. Luke explicitly describes Jesus praying with the people baptized; Matthew describes His immediate emergence from the water without the prayer detail.

Both describe dove-like Spirit descent and direct heavenly address to the beloved Son. Luke says upon Him in bodily form; Mark says into Him. Delight and well pleased remain the supplied voice wordings.

Both connect Jesus with Joseph while qualifying the relationship. Luke says as was supposed and names Heli; Matthew calls Joseph Mary's husband, names Jacob before Joseph, and says Jesus was born of Mary. Neither a maternal-line solution nor an identity of Heli and Jacob is asserted.

Both place Zerubbabel next to Shealtiel within Jesus' genealogy. Luke continues toward Neri and through Rhesa; Matthew toward Jechoniah and through Abiud. This compares the overlapping names and differing branches without declaring the full ancestries identical.

Samuel names Nathan among David's Jerusalem-born sons, corresponding to Luke's Nathan-David link. It does not independently name Melea, Menna, or Mattatha or establish their intervening links, and Nathan is not identified merely by sharing a prophet's name.

Both genealogies include David but take different onward branches: Luke names Nathan, while Matthew follows David through Solomon. The comparison records the difference rather than making the branches one or inventing a reconciliation.

The genealogies overlap in Nahshon, Boaz, Obed, and Jesse in the same succession, read in opposite directions. Luke has Sala where Ruth has Salman; that actual name difference is preserved rather than silently renamed.

Both connect Perez, Hezron, and Amminadab in the ancestral sequence. Luke includes Admin and Arni between Amminadab and Hezron, while Ruth has Arran there. The two Luke names are not treated as automatically one name-form of Arran or Ram.

Genesis gives the Nahor-Terah-Abram succession corresponding to Luke's reversed Nahor-Terah-Abraham portion. The supplied Abram and Abraham forms remain visible; this target does not independently establish Luke's Jacob-Isaac portion.

Both genealogies connect Abraham with Isaac and Jacob. Matthew continues to Judah and his brothers; Luke's verse continues farther back through Terah and Nahor. This pair supports the shared patriarchal portion without asserting identical complete genealogies.

Genesis explicitly gives the Shelah-Eber-Peleg-Reu-Serug succession, which Luke lists in reverse direction. The Genesis age statements are preserved in the target but are not turned into ages claimed by Luke.

Genesis gives Shem, Arphaxad, and Cainan, with Cainan fathering Shelah inside the original 11:13 unit. This matches the post-Flood Cainan position across Luke 3:35–36; it is not confused with the pre-Flood Cainan in Luke 3:37.

Chronicles lists Lamech, Noah, and Noah's son Shem, corresponding to that portion of Luke's reverse ancestry. The target does not supply Luke's post-Flood Cainan, so it is not treated as confirming every name in the verse.

Both lists contain the pre-Flood sequence through Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, and Methuselah, with Luke read in reverse. Chronicles has Kenan where Luke has Cainan; the name form is preserved and not confused with the post-Flood Cainan linked to Arphaxad in Luke 3:36.

Genesis describes God creating Adam, Adam fathering Seth, and Seth fathering Enosh, corresponding to Luke's final reverse ancestry. Genesis's creation wording is not recast as biological generation by God merely because Luke ends with of God.

review_notes: All 38 actual Luke 3 source units and every retained target were read from exact Saints snapshots, with context. The 31 proposed completed sources have 34 distinct pairs; seven sources remain deferred with zero credit.

Target IDs resolve, original target ranges are contiguous, complete source coverage is exact, pair keys are unique, and no target contains its own source unit. No wording or continuation structure was changed.
The unique chronological list is deferred. Repeated personal names in the unmatched six lineage units do not establish identities, filiation, or connections to famous prophetic or patriarchal names.

Luke and Matthew genealogy comparisons explicitly preserve Heli versus Jacob, Neri versus Jechoniah, Rhesa versus Abiud, and Nathan versus Solomon. No maternal-line, adoption, levirate, or other historical reconciliation is invented.

Sala versus Salman, Admin and Arni versus Arran, Cainan versus Kenan, and Abram versus Abraham remain the original English forms. The documented Abram-to-Abraham name change was checked in Genesis 17:5 as broader context without rewriting Genesis 11.

Post-Flood Cainan linked to Arphaxad in Luke 3:36 and Genesis 11:12–13 is kept distinct from the pre-Flood Cainan in Luke 3:37. The original Genesis 11:13 unit already contains the Cainan-Shelah material; it was neither split into invented verse units nor replaced with a different edition's lineage.

Partial genealogy comparisons name their scope explicitly. Samuel establishes Nathan among David's sons but does not confirm Melea, Menna, or Mattatha; Chronicles 1:3–4 supports Lamech-Noah-Shem without silently adding Cainan.

John's audience differs between Luke's crowds and Matthew's Pharisees and Sadducees. Fire in Luke's Spirit baptism and bodily form/upon Him in the baptism scene are not inserted into Mark's actual supplied wording.

Ethical parallels specify their scope: food and clothing; tax-collection extortion and restitution; or monetary contentment. Hebrews is not represented as repeating every command directed to soldiers.
